title: First and Last Aggregate Function Optimization
body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

When first or last aggregate functions are used without a keyed group by, there is still a full scan or every row. This isn't necessary and can lead to suboptimal execution time.

### Describe the solution you'd like.

When first or last is used without keyed groups, there could be an alternate execution plan that utilizes something along the lines of an order by and limit to improve the overall execution time. 

### Describe alternatives you've considered.

_No response_

### Full Name:

Nicholas Guerra

### Affiliation:

Kronus Engineering

### Additional context

### SELECT last(timestamp) FROM systemic
```
GroupBy vectorized: false
  values: [last(timestamp)]
    DataFrame
      Row forward scan
      Frame forward scan on: system_io
```
```
1 row in 139ms
Execute: 102.24ms
Network: 36.76ms 
Total: 139ms
```

### SELECT timestamp FROM system_io ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 1
```
Limit lo: 1
  DataFrame
    Row backward scan
    Frame backward scan on: system_io
```
```
1 row in 39ms
Execute: 257.21μs
Network: 38.74ms
Total: 39ms
```

comments.body:
@reporter @participant2 need a bit of clarity on this..
does **systemic** table store records in descending order of timestamp or ascending in each partition
Asking this because :
Suppose all partitions contain records in **ascending order** of timestamp
Then 
- query plan for **SELECT last(timestamp) FROM systemic** shows it is doing row and frame forward scan which means if it is scanning all records from starting and reaching the needed record after scanning all rows, which is **not optimal**, but in case of **SELECT timestamp FROM system_io ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 1** while doing a row and frame backward scan it will be reading exactly one row (last row) which **is optimal**

Suppose all partitions contain records in **descending order** of timestamp
- query plan for **SELECT last(timestamp) FROM systemic**, will be **optimal** as the latest record will be first on the frame, but in the case of **SELECT timestamp FROM system_io ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 1**  it will scan through all the rows from lowest to highest which will **not be optimal**

I am thinking along the lines of how clustered indexes work in Postgres, please correct me if I am wrong here

comments.author: participant4
comments.body: @participant3 Partitions are clustered in ascending order. Backward scans are only applied in limited cases (only ordering by timestamp and no other columns), whereas it could instead apply any time the first column in the ordering clause is the designated timestamp.

@participant4 @participant2 I did some code walkthrough basis information conveyed by you
Here's what I did
 Created a table with a designated timestamp column and debugged both queries  

Observations for query with **orderBy** on **Designated Timestamp** column
1. There is a concept of **nestedModel** 
2. There is an attribute of query model which is called **orderByAdvice** , gives info about what column (token) to use for order by clause.
3. Whether to go with FrameFwd Or Backward scan depends on this **orderByAdvice**, which is populated in **nestedModel** of baseModel (Code Ref :- https://github.com/questdb/questdb/blob/master/core/src/main/java/io/questdb/griffin/SqlOptimiser.java#L3109)
4. **selectModelType** is _SELECT_MODEL_CHOOSE_

Observations for query with **last** function on **Designated Timestamp** column
1. **NestedModel** of this query doesn't contain **orderByAdvice** due to which it is doing FrameFwd scan
2. **selectModelType** is _SELECT_MODEL_GROUP_BY_

Questions:
1. What is meant by nestedModel?
2. How should I approach solving this?

comments.author: participant4
comments.body:
@participant3 Looks like you've done some good investigating so far. I hope some of the following information is helpful as you dig deeper.

1.

Within a QueryModel, you have the nestedModel field. Each nestedModel represents a lower part of the query. Sometimes this is an actual subquery, but other times not.

You can print out the QueryModel for debugging using `.toString0()`. Depending on what step you do this at in the SqlOptimiser, you will see different things.

For example, a `SELECT` statement with a `GROUP BY` will usually produce at least three models, which are set out something like this:

`(select-choose (select-group-by (select-none))`.

2.

In terms of solving this, there are several options.

Let's look at the goal. In terms of result set, we would expect the following queries to be equivalent:

a) `SELECT last(timestamp) FROM trades` 
b) `SELECT timestamp FROM trades ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 1`
c) `SELECT timestamp FROM trades LIMIT -1`

The reason that query a) is slow is because it becomes a GROUP BY with a forward scan over the whole table.

![image](https://github.com/questdb/questdb/assets/29717167/3f00387c-a55c-465c-a062-7bc74494a004)

Whereas for b) and c), you don't have a GROUP BY. Therefore the order by advice is pushed down, and since it is ordering by designated timestamp only, you get a backwards scan.

![image](https://github.com/questdb/questdb/assets/29717167/31ccc028-eb38-48f0-9f67-880c9f62c7b7)

There are several ways to improve it. One possible route would be to add a function in SqlOptimiser (probably as a step before rewriteSelectClause) to identify queries like a). Then you would produce an output model like b).

To do that, you can breakpoint the code and look at the model when you run the query a) and then the model when you run with query b). Then when you identify query a), simply emit a new QueryModel that looks like query b).

3.

There is a related issue. Currently, a backwards scan will only be implemented if you only provide the designated timestamp in ordering, and no other columns. For example, this query gives an optimal plan:

`select timestamp, price from trades ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 1`

![image](https://github.com/questdb/questdb/assets/29717167/06ec7b22-ca6d-470d-a98d-69edb143be72)

However, if you introduce a second field in the order by, you will not generate a backward scan: 

`select timestamp, price from trades ORDER BY timestamp, price DESC LIMIT 1`

![image](https://github.com/questdb/questdb/assets/29717167/3eb2fa62-8c34-41c1-8775-435604c56a05)

This is because of this function: https://github.com/questdb/questdb/blob/aa2af8ab3122e889353867edec5e9fba831e7178/core/src/main/java/io/questdb/griffin/SqlCodeGenerator.java#L4720

A backwards scan should actually be generated any time the first column is the designated timestamp. Currently, it only works if there is the timestamp column on its own, and no other columns.

It may be worth fixing this at the same time.
